Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.

In the current study, we examined whether CD affects the risk of diabetic retinopathy (DRP) in patients with T1D. This was a population-based cohort study. Through the Swedish National Patient Register, we identified 41,566 patients diagnosed with diabetes in 1964–2009 and who were ≤30 years of age at diagnosis. CD was defined as having villous atrophy (Marsh stage 3) according to small intestinal biopsies performed between 1969 and 2008, with biopsy reports obtained from Sweden’s 28 pathology departments. During follow-up, 947 T1D patients had a diagnosis of CD. We used Cox regression analysis with CD as a time-dependent covariate to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) for DRP in patients with T1D and CD and compared them with patients with T1D but no CD. Duration of CD correlated with the risk of DRP. No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The study found that HIT-enhanced SMBG alone resulted in no change in mean HbA1c, family-centered goal setting showed a non-significant decrease of 0.3% at 6 months, and the combined approach demonstrated a significant HbA1c reduction of 0.6% at 3 months that diminished to a non-significant 0.4% reduction by 6 months, with higher baseline HbA1c levels predicting greater improvement; additionally, there were no significant changes or group differences in the daily frequency of SMBG testing. Based on these findings, the authors recommend further research into pairing family-centered goal setting with HIT-enhanced diabetes technologies, noting that family goal setting and counseling may be particularly useful when adolescents adopt new self-management technologies to achieve optimal clinical outcomes, especially among those with higher baseline HbA1c levels.

Results demonstrate that young children with type 1 diabetes exhibit widespread reductions in axial diffusivity across multiple brain regions compared to healthy controls, with microstructural changes significantly driven by chronic hyperglycemia—including elevated HbA1c levels and prolonged glucose elevations above 180, 250, and 300 mg/dL—as well as high glucose variability. Higher blood glucose metrics and erratic fluctuations correspond with decreased fractional anisotropy and increased radial diffusivity, pointing to altered myelination and axonal integrity, whereas hypoglycemic events and severe hypoglycemic seizures show no significant association with white matter structural alterations. Furthermore, fractional anisotropy levels directly correlate with Full-Scale IQ in pediatric diabetes patients, confirming the functional relevance of these white matter changes during early neurodevelopment. While the findings do not establish direct clinical practice guidelines, the clear clinical recommendation for treating pediatric type 1 diabetes is to reorient management strategies toward minimizing chronic hyperglycemia and smoothing out sharp glucose fluctuations rather than focusing predominantly on avoiding hypoglycemia, utilizing continuous glucose monitoring to actively suppress high blood sugar spikes and safeguard early brain development and cognitive potential.

By assessing children aged 6 to 18 years at baseline, day 5, day 28, and 6 months using MRI, MRS, and cognitive testing, the study highlights how DKA alters cerebral structure and neurocognitive performance even without the presence of severe clinical cerebral edema. The findings reveal that children presenting with DKA experience significant changes in white and gray matter structures, including higher total white matter volume and increased mean diffusivity in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes at presentation, alongside reduced total cortical gray matter volume and lower levels of N-acetylaspartate in the frontal gray matter and basal ganglia. Although acute structural and volume changes resolved over time, DKA presentation was associated with persistent adverse functional outcomes at the 6-month follow-up, specifically lower delayed memory recall, poorer sustained and divided attention, and reduced baseline mental state scores. Furthermore, lower blood pH at presentation and younger age were identified as key predictors of both structural brain changes and poorer neurocognitive outcomes. The recommendations and guidelines stemming from this study emphasize the critical need to view DKA-related brain injury along a continuous spectrum rather than as an isolated risk limited to overt cerebral edema. Clinicians and healthcare providers are urged to prioritize early detection and prompt intervention for Type 1 Diabetes in pediatric patients to prevent initial DKA episodes entirely, thereby protecting vulnerable developing brain tissue.
passage_3: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

CD is defined as a permanent immune-mediated response to gluten present in wheat, barley, and rye. CD has a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations that resemble a multisystemic disorder rather than an isolated intestinal disease, and is characterized by small bowel injury and the presence of specific antibodies. Detection of CD-specific antibodies (e.g., tissue transglutaminase) in the serum is very helpful for the initial screening of patients with suspicion of CD. Intestinal biopsy is required in most patients to confirm the diagnosis. A nonbiopsy strategy for the diagnosis of CD in selected children is suggested and discussed in detail. Current treatment for CD requires strict adherence to a gluten-free diet (GFD) and lifelong medical follow-up. Most patients have excellent clinical response to a GFD. Nonresponsive CD is defined by persistent or recurrent symptoms despite being on a GFD. These patients require a systematic workup to rule out specific conditions that may cause persistent or recurrent symptoms, especially unintentional gluten contamination. Refractory CD is a rare cause of nonresponsive CD often associated with poor prognosis.
passage_2: "Screening for celiac disease in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" reports that prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and celiac disease (CD) vary from 1.6% to 16.4% worldwide. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.

Regarding therapeutic management, the paper outlines guidelines based on C-peptide levels and disease characteristics. Patients with random C-peptide levels at or below 300 pmol/L require primary insulin therapy.

Furthermore, clinical and biochemical comorbidities were highly prevalent within two years of diagnosis, including low high-density lipoprotein levels in 79.8%, blood pressure at or above the 90th percentile in 26.3%, microalbuminuria in 13.0%, and elevated triglycerides in 10.2% of participants. Retinopathy risk was significantly higher among participants who were older, had a longer diabetes duration, or had higher mean HbA1c levels, whereas those in the highest body mass index (BMI) tertile unexpectedly presented with a lower prevalence. passage_3: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

Hypoglycemia was the most frequently reported adverse event, with higher rates observed in active treatment groups, though no severe hypoglycemia cases occurred. passage_1: The study "Impact of dietary protein on postprandial glycaemic control and insulin requirements in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" evaluates the glycemic impact of dietary protein and the corresponding insulin requirements for individuals living with Type 1 diabetes. By synthesizing evidence from a systematic literature search across biomedical databases, the review highlights that dietary protein significantly contributes to postprandial glycemic excursions alongside carbohydrates, leading to delayed hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the paper discusses recommendations and clinical guidelines to consider dietary protein composition—not just carbohydrate content alone—when calculating mealtime insulin doses to improve overall postprandial glycemic control.
passage_2: The study Impact of dietary protein on postprandial glycaemic control and insulin requirements in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review determines the impact of dietary protein on postprandial blood glucose levels and mealtime insulin requirements in individuals with Type 1 diabetes. Findings indicate that protein consumed alone does not exhibit a significant glycaemic effect until doses reach ≥75 g, whereas within a carbohydrate-containing meal, as little as ≥12.5 g of protein affects postprandial glucose. The timing of this glucose-raising effect ranges from 90 to 240 minutes, and combining fat with a high-protein meal further enhances the postprandial glycaemic response and increases total insulin requirements. Based on these insights, recommendations and guidelines advise that dietary protein must be explicitly taken into account alongside carbohydrates when calculating mealtime insulin doses, emphasizing the need for modified, multi-macronutrient insulin dosing strategies to prevent postprandial hyperglycaemia.
passage_3: Insulin strategies for dietary fat and protein in type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the efficacy of various insulin dosing and delivery strategies used to manage postprandial glycaemia following meals high in fat and protein in individuals living with type 1 diabetes. Synthesizing data from 18 randomized controlled trials published between 1995 and 2021, the paper finds that administering additional insulin—specifically an extra 24% to 75% of the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (ICR)—improves postprandial glucose control, whereas increases below 24% generally offer little glycaemic benefit. The findings also demonstrate that split or combination boluses outperform standard single doses, and administering insulin 15 minutes prior to the meal yields superior postprandial glycaemic outcomes. Based on these insights, the paper provides supportive guidelines and recommendations for managing high-fat and high-protein meals, advising an additional 24% to 75% ICR delivered via a combination bolus with a minimum upfront dose of 60% ICR, administered 15 minutes before eating.

The RISE Pediatric Medication Study compared two approaches-glargine followed by metformin and metformin alone-in preserving or improving β-cell function in youth with impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes during and after therapy withdrawal. Ninety-one pubertal, overweight/obese 10-19-year-old youth with IGT (60%) or type 2 diabetes of <6 months duration (40%) were randomized to either 3 months of insulin glargine with a target glucose of 4.4-5.0 mmol/L followed by 9 months of metformin or to 12 months of metformin alone. β-Cell function (insulin sensitivity paired with β-cell responses) was assessed by hyperglycemic clamp at baseline, 12 months (on treatment), and 15 months (3 months off treatment). No significant differences were observed between treatment groups at baseline, 12 months, or 15 months in β-cell function, BMI percentile, HbA1c, fasting glucose, or oral glucose tolerance test 2-h glucose results. In both treatment groups, clamp-measured β-cell function was significantly lower at 12 and 15 months versus baseline. HbA1c fell transiently at 6 months within both groups. BMI was higher in the glargine followed by metformin versus metformin alone group between 3 and 9 months. Only 5% of participants discontinued the interventions, and both treatments were well tolerated. We concluded that in youth with IGT or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes, neither 3 months of glargine followed by 9 months of metformin nor 12 months of metformin alone halted the progressive deterioration of β-cell function. Alternate approaches to preserve β-cell function in youth are needed.
passage_2: The study "RISE Pediatric Medication Study" evaluates two distinct therapeutic approaches—3 months of insulin glargine followed by 9 months of metformin versus 12 months of metformin alone—in preserving or improving β-cell function in youth aged 10–19 years with impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes during active treatment and 3 months after therapy withdrawal. The main findings indicate that neither treatment regimen significantly improved or preserved clamp-measured β-cell function, as both groups demonstrated progressive deterioration in β-cell responses at 12 and 15 months compared to baseline, with no significant differences observed between the two groups regarding β-cell function, HbA1c, fasting glucose, or oral glucose tolerance test outcomes. Based on these findings, the authors recommend that alternative therapeutic approaches and strategies beyond metformin and insulin glargine be developed to preserve β-cell function and halt disease progression in youth with dysglycemia.
passage_3: "A Clinical Trial to Maintain Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 2 Diabetes (TODAY)” study evaluates the efficacy of three treatment regimens—metformin alone, metformin combined with rosiglitazone, and metformin combined with an intensive lifestyle-intervention program—in achieving durable glycemic control among children and adolescents aged 10 to 17 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes. The study found that 45.6% of participants experienced treatment failure over an average follow-up of 3.86 years, with metformin plus rosiglitazone demonstrating superiority over metformin alone by reducing treatment failure to 38.6% compared to 51.7% for monotherapy, whereas metformin plus lifestyle intervention yielded intermediate results (46.6%) that were not significantly different from metformin alone. Subgroup analyses revealed that metformin plus rosiglitazone was particularly effective in girls, while metformin monotherapy was least effective in non-Hispanic Black participants. Serious adverse events occurred in 19.2% of participants across the trial, and although the paper does not explicitly state formal clinical recommendations or guidelines, it concludes that metformin monotherapy fails to maintain durable glycemic control in roughly half of youth with type 2 diabetes and that adding rosiglitazone provides superior glycemic durability compared to monotherapy or intensive lifestyle interventions.

Question: What were the main findings of the Let's Empower and Prepare (LEAP) Evaluation of a Structured Transition Program for Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes.txt study?

" let ' s empower and prepare ( leap ) : evaluation of a structured transition program for young adults with type 1 diabetes " evaluates the efficacy of a structured transition program compared to usual care in improving routine clinical follow - up, glycemic control, and psychosocial outcomes among young adults transitioning from pediatric to adult diabetes care. the study found that while limitations prevented direct comparisons of adult care visits with the control group, 78 % of the intervention group participants discharged from pediatric care successfully established adult care visits, and the intervention group demonstrated significantly improved glycemic control, a lower incidence of severe hypoglycemia, and better global well - being compared to the control group.

Retrieved Evidence 2:
" components of interventions that improve transitions to adult care for adolescents with type 1 diabetes " evaluates the effectiveness of various transition program components in improving health outcomes for adolescents and young adults with type 1 diabetes transferring from pediatric to adult care through a systematic review and meta - analysis of 18 studies involving 3, 382 participants. the findings indicate that while most studies reported improvement or maintenance of hemoglobin a1c levels post - transition, pooling data from controlled studies showed no significant differences in hba1c at 12 months, though transition programs demonstrated consistent success in reducing episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis. the paper notes that further research is needed to determine the most effective program types, and guidelines or explicit recommendations regarding specific program protocols were not detailed in the provided text.

" closing the gap : results of the multicenter canadian randomized controlled trial of structured transition in young adults with type 1 diabetes " evaluates the effectiveness of an 18 - month structured transition program featuring a transition coordinator on clinic attendance, glycemic control, satisfaction with care, and diabetes - related distress among young adults aged 17 to 20 with type 1 diabetes. the study found that during the intervention period, participants in the transition program had improved clinic attendance, greater satisfaction with care, and decreased diabetes - related distress compared to those receiving standard care, alongside a trend toward lower hba1c levels, though these benefits were not sustained 12 months after the intervention ended.

The recommendations and guidelines stemming from this study emphasize the critical need to view DKA-related brain injury along a continuous spectrum rather than as an isolated risk limited to overt cerebral edema. passage_1: "Predictivity of thyroid autoantibodies for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes" investigates the prevalence of thyroid autoantibodies and their significance for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes. Antibodies to thyroglobulin (anti-TG) and thyroperoxidase (anti-TPO) were measured in 216 patients (113 boys; median age 12.9 years (range 1-22 years)) with Type 1 diabetes (diabetes duration 2.5 years (0-14 years)) in a cross-sectional study. Sixteen patients with significantly elevated anti-TPO titres were followed longitudinally (6.0 years (4-13 years)) including the measurement of anti-TPO, anti-TG, T(3), T(4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and ultrasound assessment. Twenty-two patients (10.0%) had significantly elevated titres of anti-TPO, 19 (8.7%) of anti-TG and 13 (5.9%) of both autoantibodies. Girls had more frequently elevated anti-TPO antibodies than boys (P < 0.05). Eight of 16 patients (50%) developed thyroid disorders defined by a TSH elevation (> or = 4.5 microU/ml) and/or sonographic thyroid abnormalities during a median time of 3.5 years (2-6 years) after first detection of anti-TPO positivity. They were characterized by higher levels of anti-TPO (P = 0.001) and a more frequent coexistence of anti-TG antibodies (P = 0.002) than those with no development of thyroid disorder even after an observation period of 5.5 years (5-10 years). We concluded that because 50% of children with diabetes and significant titres of anti-TPO develop thyroid problems within 3-4 years, examinations of thyroid antibodies should be performed yearly. In cases of significant antibody titres, thyroid function tests and ultrasound assessment are recommended in order to minimize the risk of undiagnosed hypothyroidism in these patients.
passage_2: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.
passage_3: "Younger age at onset and sex predict celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: an Italian multicenter study" estimates the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in Italian children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes and to assess whether age at onset of type 1 diabetes is independently associated with diagnosis of celiac disease. The study group was a clinic-based cohort of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes cared for in 25 Italian centers for childhood diabetes. Yearly screening for celiac disease was performed using IgA/IgG anti-gliadin and IgA anti-endomysium antibodies. Of the 4,322 children and adolescents (age 11.8 ± 4.2 years) identified with type 1 diabetes, biopsy-confirmed celiac disease was diagnosed in 292 (prevalence 6.8%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 6.0–7.6), with a higher risk seen in girls than in boys (odds ratio [OR] 1.93, 1.51–2.47). In 89% of these, diabetes was diagnosed before celiac disease. In logistic regression analyses, being younger at onset of diabetes, being female, and having a diagnosis of a thyroid disorder were independently associated with the risk of having diabetes and celiac disease. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

passage_1: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

A retrospective case control study was performed in order to explore the effect of subclinical hypothyroidism on metabolic control in Type 1 diabetes mellitus. For this purpose each patient with Type 1 diabetes and subclinical hypothyroidism (cases) was matched for age, duration of disease and, if possible, for sex, with two to three diabetic patients without hypothyroidism (controls). Parameters of metabolic control such as HbA1c, total insulin requirement and frequency of symptomatic hypoglycaemia were retrieved for 12, 6 and 3 months before and after diagnosis of hypothyroidism. Thirteen patients (two male/11 female) patients were diagnosed with subclinical hypothyroidism and were matched with 31 controls (nine male/22 female). There was no difference (mean and range) in terms of age (11.9 years (4.4-18.1) vs. 11.7 years (3.5-18.1), P = 0.9) and duration of disease (5.1 years (1.2-10.5) vs. 4.38 years (0.9-10.8), P = 0.6) between the two groups. There was no difference in HbA1c and total insulin requirement between the two groups at any time point of assessment (anova P = 0.8 and P = 0.1, respectively). Patients with hypothyroidism had significantly more symptomatic hypoglycaemic episodes during the 12 months before diagnosis (anova P = 0.05), increasing progressively during this time period and reaching a peak at time 0 (5.5+/-0.4 vs. 1.6+/-0.1 episodes/month, P = 0.01). No difference could be detected within 6 months of starting substitution therapy (2.4+/-0.2 vs. 1.6+/-0.1 episodes/week, P = 0.8). We concluded that these data suggest that subclinical hypothyroidism is associated with an increased risk of symptomatic hypoglycaemia.

As currently no data are available on the prevalence of SCH and its potential association with lipoprotein profile in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1DM), we investigated the prevalence of SCH and associated lipid levels in young diabetic patients. Cross-sectional analysis of 22,747 children, adolescents, and young adults (age <25 years) with T1DM with normal T3 and T4 and either normal TSH (≥0.5 to <4.0 mIU/l, euthyroid group) or elevated TSH (≥4.0 to <25.0 mIU/l, SCH group) and simultaneous measurement of serum lipid and lipoprotein status. The prevalence rate of SCH in the study population was 7.2%. Adjusted for age, gender, diabetes duration, current insulin dose, HbA1c, and BMI z-score, patients with SCH had significantly higher levels of total cholesterol (178.7 vs 175.3 mg/dl, P<0.001) and LDL-cholesterol (97.0 vs 93.7 mg/dl, P<0.001) compared with euthyroid patients. We concluded that SCH is a common finding in children, adolescents, and young adults with T1DM. SCH is associated with increased levels of total cholesterol, and LDL-cholesterol adjusted for potential confounders. SCH-associated increases in lipid and lipoprotein levels may therefore add to an increased long-term cardiovascular risk in young patients with T1DM.

Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor approved for the treatment of T2DM in adults. The objective was to assess the safety and efficacy of canagliflozin in children and adolescents with T2DM. This was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03170518; EudraCT: 2016-005223-88) conducted at 104 sites in 10 countries. Participants were children and adolescents aged 10 years or older with T2DM (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c] ≥6.5% to ≤11%). Participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (100 mg) or placebo once daily. Participants with week 12 readings of 7% or higher for HbA1c and at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for estimated glomerular filtration rate were randomly assigned again at week 13 to either keep receiving 100 mg of canagliflozin (or placebo) or have their dose uptitrated to 300 mg (or placebo). The treatment period was 52 weeks. The primary efficacy end point was change in HbA1c from baseline to week 26, along with secondary efficacy end points and safety. A total of 171 participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (n = 84) or placebo (n = 87). At week 26, HbA1c reduction from baseline was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (difference in least-squares means, -0.76% [95% CI, -1.25% to -0.27%]; P = 0.002). The proportion of participants who achieved HbA1c levels below 6.5% was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (36.3% vs. 14.0%; difference, 22.3 percentage points [CI, 10.5 to 34.1 percentage points]). Treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) occurred in 77.4% and 74.7% and serious treatment-emergent AEs in 9.5% and 5.7% of participants who received canagliflozin and placebo, respectively.

The study found that empagliflozin provided a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in HbA1c baseline levels compared to placebo (-0.84%, p=0.012), whereas linagliptin did not show a statistically significant reduction (-0.34%, p=0.29). Hypoglycemia was the most frequently reported adverse event, with higher rates observed in active treatment groups, though no severe hypoglycemia cases occurred. Based on these findings, the paper suggests that empagliflozin may offer a valuable new oral treatment option for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes to address the therapeutic unmet need in this population.

This multicentre, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised phase 3 study was undertaken at 30 centres in five countries (Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Russia, and the USA). Participants aged 10-24 years with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c concentration of 6·5-11% (48-97 mmol/mol) were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo during a 24 week double-blind period, which was then followed by a 28 week open-label safety extension in which all participants received dapagliflozin.
